article.overview: The name solar particle observation instrument describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. Such an instrument measures charged particles emitted by the Sun, including the continuous low-energy solar wind and the sporadic energetic solar energetic particles (SEPs) released during solar flares and coronal mass ejections. The flown lunar examples identified in this research are Apollo-era solar wind instruments, namely a Faraday-cup spectrometer and aluminium foil collectors, and CRaTER, a radiation telescope on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. A lunar-surface energetic particle monitor has been proposed in design studies, but no flown example was found.
article.description: A solar particle observation instrument detects charged particles arriving from the Sun and measures their number, energy and, in some designs, composition. The Moon has no substantial atmosphere and no global magnetic field to deflect incoming particles, so a surface instrument can sample the particle environment directly. Three broad measurement approaches appear in the sources reviewed. Plasma instruments such as Faraday cups measure the energy distribution of low-energy solar wind ions and electrons [1][2]. Penetrating-particle telescopes, such as CRaTER and LURAD, stack detectors so that the energy a particle deposits in each layer can be used to identify it [4][5]. Foil collectors expose material to the solar wind for hours or days and return the foil to Earth for laboratory analysis of trapped gases [3][6].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Scientific purposes reported for these instruments include measuring solar wind plasma at the lunar surface, studying how the solar wind interacts with the local magnetic environment, and determining the isotopic composition of the solar wind. The Apollo 15 Solar Wind Spectrometer objectives listed in the NASA PDS archive included measuring electron charge fluxes at the lunar surface, studying the solar wind interaction with the local magnetic field, testing whether lunar limb shocks can be detected at dawn or dusk, and making simultaneous comparisons with Apollo 12 data [1]. The Apollo 15 foil experiment was described as a means of studying elemental and isotopic abundances in the solar wind [3]. CRaTER was designed to characterise the radiation environment that humans would experience on future lunar missions [4]. LURAD is proposed for radiation monitoring at the Gateway and on the lunar surface, with the aim of assessing radiation risk for people in orbit around the Moon or at its surface [5].
article.operating_principle:
The Apollo solar wind spectrometers used modulated Faraday cups. Each cup has an entrance aperture followed by a set of grids and a collector. Square-wave alternating retarding voltages on a modulator grid set the energy threshold that particles must exceed to reach the collector, so stepping through the voltages builds an energy spectrum of incoming ions and electrons. The Apollo 15 cups each carried five circular grids and a circular collector, and the collector signal records the particles that pass each energy step [1].

Foil collectors work by exposure. An aluminium foil is set on a pole facing the Sun so that solar wind ions are captured in it. At the end of the exposure the foil is detached from the pole, sealed in a Teflon bag and returned to Earth, where trapped gases are extracted and measured [6].

Penetrating-particle telescopes identify particles by how much energy they lose as they pass through successive layers of silicon and tissue-equivalent material [4]. LURAD is proposed to combine scintillators read by silicon photomultipliers, fully depleted silicon pixel sensors and silicon-on-insulator microdosimetry sensors to identify particle species and energies [5].
article.scientific_importance: Solar particles are a major part of the charged-particle environment at the lunar surface, where the Moon has no substantial atmosphere and no global magnetic field to deflect incoming particles. Apollo-era measurements provided direct readings of solar wind electrons and ions at the surface, and foil experiments provided early measurements of the isotopic composition of noble gases in the solar wind [1][3][6]. Energetic-particle measurements are needed to assess radiation exposure for crews and equipment on the lunar surface and in lunar orbit [4][5]. A surface-based monitor would measure this environment where crews and equipment would actually be exposed.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a solar particle observation instrument. The examples below are the flown and proposed designs for which this research found a source. Values are tied to the named instrument and source. Two other concepts surfaced in searches, LL-SWEPT (described in a University of Alberta MSc thesis as a 14-day lunar surface telescope) and IRADCAL (an albedo particle detector for the Turkish Lunar Mission in lunar orbit), were not examined in detail and are not treated as examples. The Apollo 12 and Apollo 15 spectrometer records list identical mass, power and dimensions, which may reflect a shared description; this has not been independently confirmed.

examples.name: Apollo Solar Wind Spectrometer, Apollo 12
examples.timeline: Sensor covers removed automatically at about 15:30 UT on 20 November 1969, which the record does not describe as deployment. Standby during a lunar night on 3 March 1976; shut down on 15 January 1977.

examples.name: Apollo Solar Wind Spectrometer, Apollo 15
examples.sensor: Seven modulated Faraday cups. Cups 1 to 6 face 60 degrees off vertical with slightly overlapping fields of view; cup 7 points vertically. Total angular field of view per cup not stated.
examples.timeline: Turned on 19:37:10 UT on 31 July 1971 with covers in place for background data. Covers removed by ground command on 2 August 1971 at 18:07:32 UT. Intermittent modulation dropouts in proton channels 13 and 14 from 5 November 1971. Science and engineering data lost 30 June 1972 (suspected high-voltage arcing); standby indefinitely; permanently commanded off 14 June 1974.

examples.name: Apollo Solar Wind Composition (SWC) foil experiment
examples.type: Historical foil collector (flown on Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15 per NTRS record; a secondary summary also lists Apollo 16)
examples.collector: Ultra-pure aluminium foil. Apollo 11 sheet about 1.4 m by 0.3 m on a telescopic pole facing the Sun (secondary summary).
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources read beyond the Apollo 11 sheet size.
examples.results: Preliminary helium and neon concentrations reported in the Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report; the abstract page read gives no numerical values. A secondary summary states helium, neon and argon isotopic compositions were measured.
examples.team: J. Geiss, F. Buehler, H. Cerutti and P. Eberhardt, University of Bern. Manufacturer not resolved across sources.

examples.name: CRaTER on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.type: Flown radiation telescope in lunar orbit (not a surface instrument)
examples.measurement: Energy deposited by solar energetic protons and galactic cosmic rays in silicon detectors and tissue-equivalent plastic.
examples.dimensions: Not verified; full-text PDF could not be read in this research.

examples.name: LURAD (proposed design study)
examples.type: Proposed; design study with Monte Carlo simulation; the abstract describes no built prototype or flight hardware
technologies: Fully depleted silicon monolithic active pixel sensors
examples.dimensions: Not given in the abstract read; full PDF not read.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The flown spectrometers share a compact deployed size of 30.5 x 28.2 x 34.5 cm as recorded in the PDS archive. The foil collector was a large, flat aluminium sheet on a telescopic pole, about 1.4 m by 0.3 m for Apollo 11, according to a secondary summary. A new instrument would need its dimensions set by its energy range, field of view and mounting requirements, which were not specified for any proposed design reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The flown Apollo spectrometers are recorded at 5.7 kg each. Mass for the foil experiment, CRaTER and LURAD was not verified. Mass drives launch and lander requirements, so the absence of verified masses for three of the five examples limits transportation assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Apollo spectrometers are recorded at 12.5 W total power each. No power figure is given for the foil experiment in the sources read, and power for CRaTER and LURAD was not verified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The lunar surface has no substantial atmosphere, so surface instruments receive solar particles directly and face large temperature swings between lunar day and night. The Apollo 12 spectrometer was placed in standby during a lunar night in March 1976 and was shut down in January 1977 to free power for the central station's thermal control [2]. The Apollo 15 spectrometer lost science and engineering data in June 1972, which analysis attributed to high-voltage arcing in its electronics [1], so high-voltage electronics need design margin for the surface environment. Foil collectors must face the Sun during exposure [6]. The CRaTER paper covers instrument testing, characterisation and calibration, which are the main performance verification steps for penetrating-particle telescopes [4]. Power is a constraint: the Apollo spectrometers drew 12.5 W in total [1][2].
article.limitations: The instruments described have different measurement goals. The Apollo spectrometers and foil experiments measure low-energy solar wind, while CRaTER and LURAD measure energetic particles. A Faraday-cup spectrometer measures only particles within its energy range and field of view [1]. The Apollo 15 spectrometer suffered modulation dropouts and then high-voltage arcing, which ended its science. Foil experiments give time-integrated results that are available only after return to Earth and laboratory analysis, so they provide no real-time information. A single surface measurement cannot determine the direction or source of an event without comparison with other data. No compatibility with any specific lander has been assessed.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Apollo-era solar wind instruments were set up by the astronauts during surface activity. The Apollo 11 foil experiment was the first experiment the crew set up on the surface [6]. The Apollo 15 spectrometer was deployed on 31 July 1971 and its covers were removed about one hour after lunar module ascent [1].
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it using a launch vehicle and transfer it towards the Moon.
Deliver the instrument to the surface with a lunar lander.
Deploy and set up the instrument, including positioning a foil collector on a pole facing the Sun [6].
Connect power and data interfaces and manage thermal and mechanical interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo-era instruments were set up by astronauts during extravehicular surface activity. Covers on the Apollo 15 spectrometer were removed by ground command after lunar module ascent [1]. Foil collectors were mounted on a telescopic pole and removed at the end of exposure [6]. No deployment method is verified for a proposed instrument.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 11 to 15 solar wind experiments are historical examples of astronaut-deployed surface instruments [1][3][6]. CRaTER on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter is an orbital example [4]. LURAD is a proposed example for both the Gateway and the lunar surface [5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft has not been assessed, because no verified interface evidence was found. The Apollo 15 spectrometer's 5.7 kg mass and 30.5 x 28.2 x 34.5 cm deployed size are the transportation-relevant figures verified in this research [1].

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 15 and Apollo 12 spectrometers made direct measurements of solar wind electrons and ions at the lunar surface [1][2]. The Apollo 11 foil experiment was among the first experiments set up on the surface, and according to a secondary summary it gave the first measurements of the solar wind's noble-gas composition [6]. Preliminary helium and neon results were presented in the Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report [3]. CRaTER is the flown energetic-particle telescope described in this research, but its mission results and the current operational status of LRO were not checked [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name solar particle observation instrument does not specify an energy range, a measurement type or a mission. The flown examples measure very different things: the Apollo Faraday-cup spectrometers record low-energy solar wind plasma, the foils return time-integrated samples for laboratory analysis, and CRaTER records energetic particles from orbit. Values such as mass, dimensions, power and sensor response must be tied to a named instrument and source. Several figures in this article come from secondary summaries and have not been checked against primary publications.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No images were included because no direct image asset could be verified from an official source page in this research.

data_quality_notes: Apollo 15 SWS figures (energy ranges, flux range, cadence, mass, power, dimensions, timeline, objectives) come from the NASA PDS instrument description read directly.

Apollo 12 SWS figures come from the PDS catalogue record read directly. Its mass, power and dimensions are identical to the Apollo 15 record and have not been independently confirmed. Deployment date is not explicitly given; 20 November 1969 is the cover-removal date.

Apollo Solar Wind Composition foil dimensions, exposure times, Apollo 16 flight and Apollo 11 first-on-surface claims come from secondary summaries (a Wikipedia article and search-result summaries), not primary sources.
The NTRS Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report page gave no numerical helium or neon concentrations and no foil dimensions.

The CRaTER paper full text was not readable in this research; its description is drawn from search-result summaries. The Schwadron et al. 2012 result seen in search was not used because its citation could not be verified.
LURAD details are from the arXiv abstract only; the full PDF was not read. Mass, dimensions, power and data rate are not given in the abstract.
LL-SWEPT (University of Alberta MSc thesis) and IRADCAL (Turkish Lunar Mission albedo detector) were identified from search summaries only and are not treated as examples.
No direct image asset was verified. ESA image page returned HTTP 404; Smithsonian object and Smithsonian Magazine pages returned HTTP 403. The article therefore contains no images.
One web search result contained embedded instructions unrelated to this topic. They were ignored and not acted upon.
LRO current operational status was not checked. Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and not included.
